title: The Mark on the Foreheads
summary: God summons six executioners and a man clothed in linen carrying a writing kit. The glory of God moves from the cherubim to the threshold of the temple, and the man in linen is sent to mark the foreheads of everyone who sighs and groans over the city's abominations. The executioners follow, beginning at the sanctuary, and strike down all who are unmarked. Ezekiel falls on his face and pleads for the remnant, but God answers that the guilt of the land is exceedingly great.
story: The vision that began in chapter 8 continues without a break. Chapter 8 ended with God's verdict on what Ezekiel had seen in the temple; chapter 9 shows the verdict carried out, in visionary form, a few years before the Babylonian army actually took the city. The chapter also introduces a movement that will dominate chapters 9 to 11: the glory of the God of Israel begins to leave. Here it rises from above the cherubim in the inner sanctuary and moves to the threshold of the temple (verse 3). In chapter 10 it will pause at the east gate, and in chapter 11 it will leave the city altogether. Between those steps, the book keeps asking the question Ezekiel cries out in verse 8: will anyone be left?
historical:
The vision is part of the experience dated in 8:1 to 592 BC, while Ezekiel was in Babylon. The destruction it portrays came in 587 or 586 BC, when the Babylonians broke through Jerusalem's walls, killed many of its inhabitants, and burned the temple (2 Kings 25:8-10; Jeremiah 52). Ezekiel presents that coming military disaster as God's own act of judgment, carried out by agents he commands. In the vision the executioners are heavenly figures; in history the destroyers would be Babylonian soldiers.

The mark of protection has a real parallel in Jeremiah's time. Jeremiah records that some people in Jerusalem were spared at the fall, among them the Cushite official Ebed-melech, who had rescued Jeremiah from a cistern (Jeremiah 39:15-18). Ezekiel's vision puts the same principle in picture form: God distinguishes those who grieve over evil from those who practice it.
cultural:
The man in linen belongs to the priestly world. Linen was the fabric of priestly garments (Leviticus 16:4), and in later visions heavenly messengers are also clothed in linen (Daniel 10:5). The writing kit at his waist was the standard equipment of an ancient scribe: a case holding reed pens and a small supply of ink. His task, marking foreheads, draws on the ancient practice of marking slaves or devotees as belonging to a master or a god, and on Israel's own memory of the Passover, when blood on the doorposts marked the houses the destroyer would pass over (Exodus 12:13, 23).

The mark itself is the Hebrew letter tav, the last letter of the alphabet. In the old Hebrew script used in Ezekiel's day, tav was written as a simple X or a cross-shaped stroke. Some early Christian writers later saw in it a sign of the cross. That is a later Christian reflection; in Ezekiel the mark simply means ownership and protection. The scene also locates the executioners by the bronze altar (verse 2), the great altar of sacrifice in the temple court, so that judgment begins at the place of atonement.
literary: The chapter is a short, tightly written scene with speech and action alternating. God calls (verse 1), the agents appear (verse 2), the glory moves (verse 3), orders are given in two sets, one for the marker and one for the executioners (verses 4 to 7), the prophet intercedes (verse 8), God answers (verses 9 and 10), and the man in linen reports that the task is done (verse 11). The frame is formal, like a report to a king. The key phrase “begin at My sanctuary” (verse 6) turns the holiest place into the starting point of judgment, reversing everything a worshiper would expect. The elders' words from 8:12 are repeated in verse 9 in reverse order, “The LORD has forsaken the land; the LORD does not see,” tying the judgment directly to the unbelief exposed in chapter 8.

outline.t: Six executioners and a man clothed in linen
The glory moves to the threshold, and the faithful are marked
The prophet pleads, and God answers
The man in linen reports: it is done

doctrines.note: Judgment here is discriminating. Before any executioner moves, the faithful are marked and protected. God does not sweep away the righteous with the wicked (compare Genesis 18:25), and those who grieve over evil are not treated as its authors.

Ezekiel falls on his face and pleads for the remnant (verse 8), standing in the tradition of Abraham and Moses as an intercessor. God does not rebuke the prayer, though his answer is hard. Intercession for a guilty people is part of the prophet's calling.

The glory's movement from the cherubim to the threshold shows that a holy God withdraws from a place given over to idols. Judgment beginning at the sanctuary means that the people closest to God's presence are held to the highest account.

words.note: Tav, mark. It is the name of the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which in the old script looked like an X. Here it is a sign of ownership and protection placed on the forehead. The same idea appears in Revelation, where God's servants are sealed on their foreheads before judgment falls (Revelation 7:3).

Anach, to sigh. It describes an audible expression of grief or distress. Those who are marked are not described as sinless but as people who sigh over what they see. Their grief is the evidence that they have not made peace with the city's evil.

Anaq, to groan, a close partner of the previous word. The pairing of sighing and groaning intensifies the picture: the faithful feel the city's sin as a wound. In a city that says God does not see, they see and they mourn.

Kavod, glory. In verse 3 the glory rises from above the cherubim, where it had rested in the inner sanctuary over the ark, and moves to the threshold. This is the first step of the departure that the next two chapters complete.

christ: Several threads here lead to Christ. The mark on the foreheads recalls the Passover blood that protected Israel's firstborn, which the New Testament connects to Christ, “our Passover lamb” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Revelation takes up Ezekiel's image directly, describing God's servants sealed on their foreheads (Revelation 7:3; 14:1) as belonging to God and the Lamb. And the principle that judgment begins at God's sanctuary is repeated in 1 Peter 4:17, which says judgment begins with the household of God. These links are the New Testament drawing on Ezekiel's pattern, not a hidden prediction in the text.

hard.q: How can God command the killing of old men, women, and children, even in a vision?
hard.a: This is one of the hardest passages in the prophets, and it should not be read quickly. The vision portrays the coming fall of Jerusalem, in which the Babylonian army did kill young and old alike, and it interprets that historical catastrophe as God's judgment rather than as a meaningless accident. Some readers therefore take the language as prophetic depiction of real events, not a pattern for any human action. Others emphasize the mark: in the vision, no one who grieved over the city's evil is harmed, which shows that the judgment is not indiscriminate. Still others note that the prophet himself cries out against the scale of it (verse 8), and that Scripture includes his protest. None of these fully removes the difficulty. What the chapter does not do is present the slaughter as something to celebrate or imitate; it presents it as the terrible cost of a people's long refusal of God.

questions: The faithful were marked because they sighed and groaned over the evil around them. What do you grieve over in your community, and what have you stopped noticing?
Ezekiel pleaded for the remnant even while receiving a vision of judgment. Whom do you find it hard to pray for?
Judgment began at the sanctuary. What does it mean for churches and religious leaders to be held to the highest standard?
